lesson.arabic-literary-selection.title_en: Choosing a text: قِصَّةٌ قَصِيرَةٌ, رِوَايَة, طَبْعَة
lesson.arabic-literary-selection.family_en: The words for literary texts, and what to find before you read for style
steps: Start with something short and complete: a قِصَّةٌ قَصِيرَةٌ, a short story, or one مَشْهَد, scene, rather than a whole رِوَايَة, novel.
Note the مُؤَلِّف, author, the طَبْعَة, edition, and the عَصْر, period: they tell you what kind of Arabic to expect.
Before style, find who tells the story, where and when it happens, and what the problem is.
Older prose and modern prose need different help: look for a glossary or a commentary that suits the period.

examples.ar: فَتَحَتْ سَلْمَى النَّافِذَةَ، فَدَخَلَ صَوْتُ الْمَطَرِ.
examples.en: Salmā opened the window, and the sound of the rain came in.
The story is set in a small village.
I read the novel in a recent edition.

why.q_en: Why تَدُورُ الْقِصَّةُ فِي, literally "the story turns in", for "is set in"?
why.a_en: دَارَ, to turn or revolve, is the usual verb for where a story happens: تَدُورُ الْأَحْدَاثُ فِي مَدِينَةٍ سَاحِلِيَّةٍ, the events take place in a coastal town.

selftest.why_en: A short story is a قِصَّةٌ قَصِيرَةٌ.

selftest.q_en: What does تَدُورُ الْقِصَّةُ فِي قَرْيَةٍ mean?
choices: the story is set in a village
the story is about a farmer
selftest.answer: the story is set in a village
selftest.why_en: دَارَ, to turn, is used for where a story happens.

leads_to.en: Who tells the story, and who speaks in it.

lesson.arabic-narrator-character.title_en: Who speaks? الرَّاوِي, الشَّخْصِيَّة, كَانَ قَدْ
lesson.arabic-narrator-character.family_en: Telling narrator, characters and author apart, and following shifts in time
steps: Keep three voices apart: الرَّاوِي, the narrator; each شَخْصِيَّة, character, in their own words; and the author, who may share neither view.
Speech verbs show who's talking: قَالَ يُوسُفُ, Yūsuf said. A colon or quotation marks then give his own words; after قَالَ, إِنَّ can report them in the narrator's words instead.
Shifts in time show in the verbs and the time words: كَانَ قَدْ with a past verb is "had done", and بَعْدَ سَنَوَاتٍ, years later, jumps ahead.
If it's unclear who a pronoun refers to, say so and give the possibilities, rather than picking one silently.

examples.en: Yūsuf said he would write to her.

examples.ar: كَانَ قَدْ سَافَرَ قَبْلَ وُصُولِ الرِّسَالَةِ.
examples.en: He had left before the letter arrived.
Years later, he went back to the village.

why.q_en: Why كَانَ قَدْ سَافَرَ for "he had travelled"?
why.a_en: كَانَ moves the time back, and قَدْ with a past verb marks the action as already done by then: he had already left. Narrators use it to step back before the main events.

selftest.why_en: The voice that tells the story, which isn't always the author's.

selftest.q_en: What does كَانَ قَدْ سَافَرَ mean?
selftest.why_en: كَانَ moves the time back, and قَدْ marks it as done.

leads_to.en: Writing about a character, with evidence from the text.

lesson.arabic-imagery-style.title_en: Images in a text: تَشْبِيه, اِسْتِعَارَة, الْمَعْنَى الْحَرْفِيُّ
lesson.arabic-imagery-style.family_en: Simile, metaphor and the other tools of style, and reading them with care
steps: Read الْمَعْنَى الْحَرْفِيُّ, the literal meaning, first: what is actually said?
A تَشْبِيه, simile, compares openly, with كَـ or مِثْلَ, like: كَانَ صَوْتُهُ كَالرَّعْدِ, his voice was like thunder.
An اِسْتِعَارَة, metaphor, gives one thing another's action or name without the comparing word: اِبْتَلَعَ الضَّجِيجُ صَوْتَهَا, the noise swallowed her voice.
Then say what the image does in its scene, and back your reading with the text. There may be more than one good reading.

why.q_en: What's the difference between كَالرَّعْدِ and a metaphor?
why.a_en: كَالرَّعْدِ says openly that his voice is like thunder: that's a تَشْبِيه. An اِسْتِعَارَة names only one side and drops the comparison: اِبْتَلَعَ الضَّجِيجُ صَوْتَهَا gives the noise a creature's act of swallowing, with no creature named. رَعْدُ صَوْتِهِ, the thunder of his voice, still names both sides, so Arabic rhetoric counts it as a compressed simile, a تَشْبِيهٌ بَلِيغٌ.

selftest.why_en: It compares openly, with a comparing word.
حَرْفِيّ is word for word, from حَرْف, a letter.

selftest.q_en: What does كَـ mean in كَالرَّعْدِ?
selftest.why_en: It's the comparing word of a simile.

leads_to.en: Writing about an image's effect, with evidence from the text.

lesson.arabic-poetry-entry.title_en: Reading a poem: قَصِيدَة, قَافِيَة, وَزْن
lesson.arabic-poetry-entry.family_en: The words for a poem's parts, and where to start
steps: Start with what the poem says: who speaks, to whom, and what happens, line by line.

A classical line has two halves, each a شَطْر, held together by وَزْن, metre, with the same قَافِيَة, rhyme, at the end of every line. شِعْرٌ حُرٌّ, free verse, keeps the metrical foot but varies the line's length, and gives up the single rhyme.
Poets may bend the usual word order, and even a word's form, for metre and rhyme: a ضَرُورَةٌ شِعْرِيَّةٌ, poetic licence. Put the words back in order to understand them.
Metre is heard, not seen: listen to a good reading before you try to name it.

examples.en: The poet wrote a poem about the sea.
The poem has one metre and one rhyme.
The morning opens a window for hope.

why.q_en: Why can't you see the metre in a translation?
why.a_en: Metre is a pattern of long and short syllables in the Arabic sounds. A translation keeps the meaning but loses the sounds, so listen to the poem read well.

selftest.why_en: The same ending sound at the end of every line.

selftest.q_en: Where do you find a poem's metre?
choices: in the sounds of the Arabic
selftest.answer: in the sounds of the Arabic
selftest.why_en: It's a pattern of long and short syllables.

lesson.arabic-literary-review.title_en: Writing about a text: أَرَى أَنَّ, يَدُلُّ عَلَى, مِثَالُ ذَلِكَ
lesson.arabic-literary-review.family_en: A claim, evidence from the text, and how the two connect

table.en: I think that, in my view

steps: State your claim about the text: أَرَى أَنَّ, I think that, introduces it.
Back it with دَلِيل, evidence, from the text: an event, a word choice, a repetition. مِثَالُ ذَلِكَ, an example of this, introduces it.
Explain how the evidence supports the claim: يَدُلُّ عَلَى, it shows.
Consider قِرَاءَةٌ أُخْرَى, another reading. Keep any اِقْتِبَاس, quotation, short, and only summarise as much of the plot as the reader needs.

examples.ar: أَرَى أَنَّ الْبَطَلَ يَخَافُ مِنَ الْوَحْدَةِ.
examples.en: I think the hero is afraid of being alone.
His long silence shows his sadness.

examples.ar: مِثَالُ ذَلِكَ أَنَّهُ يَتْرُكُ الْحَفْلَ مُبَكِّرًا.
examples.en: An example of this is that he leaves the party early.

why.q_en: Why يَخَافُ مِنَ الْوَحْدَةِ, with مِنْ?
why.a_en: خَافَ, to fear, takes مِنْ before what is feared: يَخَافُ مِنَ الظَّلَامِ, he's afraid of the dark. It can also take its object directly: يَخَافُ الظَّلَامَ.

selftest.why_en: It links evidence to a claim.

selftest.q_en: What is a دَلِيل in a literary response?
selftest.why_en: An event, a word choice or a repetition.
